question.knowledge_point: Finding the Domain Where a Partial Derivative Exists
question.problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)}{x+y},$ find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ exists.
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}z & >0\,\text{and}\,x+y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0\}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+y}\cdot \frac{1}{z} \\  & =\frac{1}{z(x+y)}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}z(x+y) & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0\}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $z$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0\}\cap \{(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0\} \\  & =\{(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0\}.\end{aligned}
$$

judgment.reasoning: Each final answer agrees with its own captured worked solution. q-36623: f_y=-x/(x²+y²) wherever the original function is defined, namely y≠0. Its simplified expression extends to some points with y=0, but the partial derivative of the original function does not exist there. q-132639: f_z=1/[z(x+y)] exists precisely where z>0 and x+y≠0; allowing negative z in the rational expression does not extend the domain of ln(z). q-132655: the exponential and all its derivatives exist for every real x, while division by y requires y≠0. q-65252: ln(xy) requires xy>0, which already implies y≠0; both stated partial derivatives exist throughout that domain. The source's intermediate references to larger derivative domains describe domains of the displayed expressions rather than domains of the actual partial derivatives; its final intersections correctly retain the original function domains.
